questions.question: How does routing work in Angular, and how do you navigate between routes?
questions.title: Angular Routing Basics
questions.direct_answer: Angular's router maps URL paths to components, so navigating to a path displays a specific component inside a <router-outlet>. You configure routes in a Routes array (path → component), register them with RouterModule, use routerLink for declarative links (the Angular equivalent of <a href>), and Router.navigate() for imperative navigation. The router handles browser URL changes, lazy-loads route modules for performance, and passes route parameters (/:id) that a component reads via ActivatedRoute.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand routes (path→component), routerLink for links, router-outlet as the mount point, and how to read route params (ActivatedRoute).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using href instead of routerLink (causes a full page reload), or forgetting <router-outlet> (nothing renders).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Routes map path→component; routerLink is the declarative link; router-outlet is where the component renders; ActivatedRoute reads params.

sections.title: Routing Maps URLs to Components
sections.content: Angular's router lets a single-page app simulate multiple pages by mapping URL paths to components. You define a Routes array pairing a path with a component, register it via RouterModule, and place a <router-outlet> in the host component where the matched route's component will render. For navigation, use routerLink (a directive on <a> tags that updates the URL without a full reload) for declarative links, and the Router service's navigate() method for imperative navigation from code. The router also supports route parameters (/:id), which a component reads via the ActivatedRoute service, and lazy loading of route modules for performance.

sections.title: How a Route Renders
sections.content:
The URL matches a route; that route's component renders inside <router-outlet>.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[URL: /users/42] --> R[Router matches path 'users/:id']
  R --> O[<router-outlet>]
  O --> C[UserDetailComponent renders]
  C -.reads.-> A[ActivatedRoute -> id: 42]
```

sections.title: Routes, routerLink, router-outlet, and params
Common Mistakes
items: Using href instead of routerLink — href causes a full page reload, defeating the SPA router.
Forgetting <router-outlet> in the host — the matched component has nowhere to render.
Not subscribing to paramMap (or not unsubscribing) when reading route params.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Angular's router maps URL paths to components; navigating to a path renders that component in a <router-outlet>.
Configure routes as a path→component array; register with RouterModule.
Use routerLink for declarative links (no full reload — never use href in an SPA).
<router-outlet> is the mount point where the matched route's component renders.
Read route params (:id) via ActivatedRoute.paramMap in the component.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Angular's router lets a single-page app behave like multiple pages by mapping URL paths to components. You define a Routes array that pairs a path with a component, register it with RouterModule, and place a router-outlet in the host component where the matched route's component renders. For navigation you use routerLink, a directive on anchor tags that updates the URL without a full reload — this is the Angular equivalent of href but without the page reload, so you should never use href in an Angular SPA. For imperative navigation from code you use the Router service's navigate method. The router also supports route parameters, like a users-slash-id path, which a component reads via the ActivatedRoute service's paramMap. The common mistakes are using href instead of routerLink, which causes a full page reload, forgetting the router-outlet so the matched component has nowhere to render, and not handling subscriptions when reading route params.
